{"id": "33:56/q13", "question": "What wording did the Prophet teach for ṣalāt?", "turns_on": "Whether the taught form is exclusive, ideal, or illustrative.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q13/p1", "position": "The Abrahamic formula asks God to bless Muhammad and his family as Abraham and his family.", "reasons": "Reports vary by including wives, descendants, household, servant and messenger, and 'us with them.' Ibn Kathir calls the corpus numerous and mass-transmitted, while grading individual routes differently."}, {"id": "33:56/q13/p2", "position": "A longer invocation asks for mercy, blessings and the Praised Station.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿud urges beauty because a prayer may be presented to the Prophet. Ali's extended version has an unknown transmitter who did not meet Ali, according to al-Mizzi."}, {"id": "33:56/q13/p3", "position": "The minimal explicit request 'O God, bless Muhammad' suffices.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says every taught formula contains this; Ibn Hajar accepts an intended supplication, while al-Nishaburi requires addressing God and rejects a first-person assertion."}, {"id": "33:56/q13/p4", "position": "Other eloquent formulas clearly expressing his honor may suffice.", "reasons": "A group of Companions and later scholars allow variations; al-Alusi says several transmitted forms can be combined and a request is better than a bare declaration."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q14", "question": "What did the Companions seek when they asked how to pray?", "turns_on": "Whether the question concerned manner alone or also meaning.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q14/p1", "position": "They asked for its manner and suitable form.", "reasons": "Al-Baji, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi favor this: they knew greeting but needed to know how believers should honor one already honored by God and angels."}, {"id": "33:56/q14/p2", "position": "They sought meaning as well as a fixed textual formula.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi records an alternative in which they wanted transmitted instruction rather than analogy."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q15", "question": "Why should believers pray for one already honored by God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q15/p1", "position": "It rewards and purifies believers who cannot repay the Prophet's due.", "reasons": "Razi says he does not need human prayer and God rewards believers out of mercy; he also prays for the community in 9:103. Al-Wasiti and others say the Prophet's due exceeds repayment."}, {"id": "33:56/q15/p2", "position": "It increases his rank and thereby the community's.", "reasons": "Bursevi cites Rumi: the follower's rank depends on the rank of the one followed."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q16", "question": "How often is ṣalāt legally required?", "turns_on": "Whether the unrestricted imperative repeats and how strongly warning reports bind.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q16/p1", "position": "Once in a lifetime, with more recommended.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa, Malik and Qadi Iyad say an unrestricted command does not require repetition. Ibn Kathir calls the lifetime-only view strange given many occasions."}, {"id": "33:56/q16/p2", "position": "At every mention of the Prophet.", "reasons": "Al-Karkhi, al-Tahawi, Ibn Kathir and Elmalili cite warning reports. Al-Alusi gives objections from alleged earlier consensus, burden and observed practice, then answers several of them."}, {"id": "33:56/q16/p3", "position": "Once per gathering despite repeated mentions.", "reasons": "Some analogize to recitation prostration or responding to a sneeze; a gathering without remembrance and prayer incurs regret or punishment."}, {"id": "33:56/q16/p4", "position": "Frequent invocation is emphatic sunnah or recommendation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya urges it at all times; Ibn ʿAshur finds no early every-mention recitation or writing practice."}, {"id": "33:56/q16/p5", "position": "At supplication's beginning and end, or often without a fixed number.", "reasons": "Some jurists require the paired supplication setting; Ibn Bukayr requires frequent invocation but sets no count."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q17", "question": "Is ṣalāt a condition of ritual prayer?", "turns_on": "How the verse and graded hadiths bear on prayer validity.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q17/p1", "position": "Yes, especially in the final tashahhud.", "reasons": "Al-Shafiʿi, Ahmad's later view, Ishaq and Ibn al-Mawwaz are cited. Ibn Kathir and al-Alusi reject a supposed consensus against it; authorities differ on deliberate versus forgetful omission."}, {"id": "33:56/q17/p2", "position": "No; it is recommended or the tashahhud greeting suffices.", "reasons": "Abu Hanifa and Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi are cited. Al-Khattabi alleges lack of early precedent; Ibn Kathir notes the 'no prayer without blessing' report has an abandoned transmitter."}, {"id": "33:56/q17/p3", "position": "The exact taught form or prayer for his family is also obligatory.", "reasons": "Some Hanbalis require exact wording; some Shafiʿis require mention of family, though Ibn Kathir says most disagree."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q18", "question": "Which formula fulfills a vow to bless him in the best manner?", "turns_on": "Whether the taught formula alone counts as best.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q18/p1", "position": "The Abrahamic form taught to the Companions.", "reasons": "Al-Nawawi says only it fulfills such a vow; al-Subki says its performance and reward are certain."}, {"id": "33:56/q18/p2", "position": "A superlative or expansive alternative form.", "reasons": "Al-Marwazi, Qadi Husayn, al-Barizi, Kamal ibn al-Humam and Ibn Hajar offer differing forms or selections."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q19", "question": "Should ṣalāt be said at slaughter?", "turns_on": "Whether 94:4 extends to slaughter despite no specific Prophetic instruction.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q19/p1", "position": "Yes, it is recommended alongside God's name.", "reasons": "Some infer it from 94:4, read to mean that God is not mentioned without the Prophet."}, {"id": "33:56/q19/p2", "position": "No, the majority reserves slaughter for mention of God alone.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir compares eating, entering and intercourse, where no Prophetic instruction to bless the Prophet exists."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q20", "question": "Which occasions especially invite ṣalāt?", "turns_on": "The transmitted practice and strength of reports for each setting.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q20/p1", "position": "Friday and its eve.", "reasons": "Angels witness the day and prayers are presented. Ibn Kathir authenticates one report, calls Abu al-Darda's route interrupted and another Friday route weak."}, {"id": "33:56/q20/p2", "position": "Mosques, pilgrimage, travel, teaching, writing and other occasions.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir gives reports and gradings for grave visits, talbiya, Safa and Marwa, slaughter, ear ringing and writing. Bursevi adds travel and teaching; Ibn ʿAshur recommends books and letters."}, {"id": "33:56/q20/p3", "position": "Supplication, call to prayer, Witr, funeral and Eid prayer.", "reasons": "Fadala's sound report puts blessing between praise and petition; Umar says a supplication is suspended without it. Other reports concern al-wasīla and ordered prayer rites."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q21", "question": "What rewards or threats do reports attach to ṣalāt?", "turns_on": "Reports differ in number, benefit, threat and chain strength.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q21/p1", "position": "Angels pray for practitioners and curse or withhold prayer from neglecters.", "reasons": "Warning reports call neglect miserliness, disgrace or a cause of loss. Ibn Kathir finds a two-angel grave route severely weak; other individual warnings receive varied gradings."}, {"id": "33:56/q21/p2", "position": "One invocation commonly earns ten divine prayers, with additions of ten deeds, removed sins or degrees.", "reasons": "Abu Talha, Abu Hurayra, Umar and Anas transmit tenfold versions; some add ten good deeds, erased sins or raised degrees, and Ibn Kathir states several chain gradings."}, {"id": "33:56/q21/p3", "position": "Frequent prayer brings nearness, intercession, sufficiency or love.", "reasons": "Ibn Masʿud's nearness report is called hasan gharīb; Ubayy's graded report promises relief when he devotes his prayer to the Prophet. Other reports mention al-wasīla and the Praised Station."}, {"id": "33:56/q21/p4", "position": "One invocation earns seventy divine and angelic prayers.", "reasons": "Abd Allah ibn Amr reports this larger number in Ibn Kathir."}, {"id": "33:56/q21/p5", "position": "Ten morning invocations earn a daily reward equal to the deeds of earth's inhabitants.", "reasons": "A report through Abu Bakr gives this exceptional reward for a specific repeated formula."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q22", "question": "How do blessings and greetings reach the Prophet after death?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q22/p1", "position": "They reach him wherever offered, by presentation or angels.", "reasons": "Friday reports say prophets' bodies are not consumed; other reports describe traveling angels, named presentation, hearing near the grave, and his returned greeting. Ibn Kathir questions several chains, especially an interrupted Abu al-Darda route and a report through an abandoned transmitter."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q23", "question": "What does taslīm command?", "turns_on": "Whether the imperative prescribes greeting, obedience or both.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q23/p1", "position": "Greet the Prophet with peace or pray for his safety.", "reasons": "Most cite the Islamic greeting; al-Alusi favors safety from harms and defects, while Ibn ʿAshur says believers address him directly because they already knew the greeting."}, {"id": "33:56/q23/p2", "position": "Submit to his commands, judgment and law.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi, Abu Abdillah and others explain obedience; Biqaʿi's ellipsis permits both greeting and submission. Al-Alusi acknowledges this but favors the greeting on report evidence."}, {"id": "33:56/q23/p3", "position": "Inwardly recogn

{"id": "33:56/q24", "question": "What does salām itself mean?", "turns_on": "Whether salām is a verbal noun, a divine name or a request for obedience.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q24/p1", "position": "Safety, peace and protection from harm.", "reasons": "Al-Qazzaz includes assurance against harm, divine safety and mercy; Ibn ʿAshur traces greeting from mutual security to courtesy and cites al-Nabigha."}, {"id": "33:56/q24/p2", "position": "The divine name al-Salām and God's guardianship.", "reasons": "Ibn Furak defines the name as God's freedom from defect; other interpretations supply blessing, protection, or an omitted word for preservation."}, {"id": "33:56/q24/p3", "position": "Peaceable non-opposition that brings submission to his law.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi records this reading but prefers safety and greeting."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q25", "question": "Why is taslīman added?", "turns_on": "Whether emphasis is grammatical or especially contextual.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q25/p1", "position": "It is an emphatic cognate accusative urging full greeting.", "reasons": "Razi, al-Zarkashi, al-Suyuti and Ibn ʿAshur give the grammatical account. Ibn al-Qayyim says prayer already has emphasis from inna and the angels; Ibn ʿAshur says taṣliya was avoided due to its burning sense."}, {"id": "33:56/q25/p2", "position": "It emphasizes believers' special need to avoid harming him.", "reasons": "Al-Khafaji relates it to the preceding harm passage; another explanation fears that without explicit emphasis greeting might seem superseded."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q26", "question": "How are prayer and greeting ordered and related?", "turns_on": "Why the second command follows prayer.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q26/p1", "position": "Prayer comes first as superior; both display honor.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashi asserts superiority. Biqaʿi and al-Alusi analyze ellipsis across the clauses."}, {"id": "33:56/q26/p2", "position": "Greeting is separately commanded because believers must explicitly submit and avoid harm.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi prefers this explanation, though he records a difficulty with saying divine and angelic prayer already entails greeting."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q27", "question": "Must ṣalāt and salām be paired?", "turns_on": "Whether paired commands require a paired utterance.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q27/p1", "position": "Pairing is preferred; separation is disliked or less preferable.", "reasons": "Al-Nawawi infers pairing from the verse; Ibn Hajar al-Haytami limits the dislike to contrary-to-better. Al-Alusi values early usage but denies the verse mandates simultaneity."}, {"id": "33:56/q27/p2", "position": "Each may be said separately.", "reasons": "Al-Hamawi reports the Hanafi view; some distinguish speech from writing. Al-Alusi says morning prayer and evening greeting fulfill the two absolute commands."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q28", "question": "May ṣalāt or salām be given independently to others?", "turns_on": "Whether examples authorize independent formulas or custom reserves them.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q28/p1", "position": "Others may be included with the Prophet, but isolated use is disliked.", "reasons": "Custom reserves the formula as a prophetic honorific. Al-Nawawi prefers mild dislike; Ibn ʿAshur and others connect it to social distinctions and sectarian usage."}, {"id": "33:56/q28/p2", "position": "Yes, believers may receive it independently.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf invokes 33:43 and 9:103; Qadi Iyad and others cite prophetic prayer for almsgivers, families and a woman with her husband."}, {"id": "33:56/q28/p3", "position": "Independent use is prohibited, though dependent use is allowed.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz reserve it for prophets. Al-Bayhaqi distinguishes honorific usage from ordinary supplication; some Hanbalis distinguish general prayer from exclusive slogans."}, {"id": "33:56/q28/p4", "position": "Other prophets and possibly angels may receive ṣalāt.", "reasons": "A prophetic report about other messengers has weak routes according to Ibn Kathir; al-Alusi accepts acting on them here. Angels are included by inference if they count as messengers."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q29", "question": "May mercy or forgiveness be requested for the Prophet?", "turns_on": "Whether prophetic honorific convention restricts ordinary supplication.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q29/p1", "position": "Mercy may be requested even by itself.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites the Bedouin's prayer and the majority; Ibn Hajar al-Haytami says the Prophet's approval overrides a general implication."}, {"id": "33:56/q29/p2", "position": "Mercy should accompany blessing or greeting, or be avoided alone.", "reasons": "Qadi Iyad reports most Malikis' restriction; al-Qurtubi, al-Suyuti and al-Ghazali distinguish prophetic honorific prayer from general mercy, citing 24:63."}, {"id": "33:56/q29/p3", "position": "Standalone forgiveness or pardon is best avoided.", "reasons": "Al-Tahtawi and al-Alusi worry it suggests deficiency, while admitting it can ask for higher rank rather than imply sin."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q30", "question": "What variant wording is reported for the verse?", "turns_on": "Whether the additions are readings, explanatory expansions or transmission claims.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q30/p1", "position": "Al-Hasan reads faṣallū with an added fāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinni prefers the common bare imperative as stronger; Ibn ʿAtiyya says the fāʾ makes the conditional link clearer."}, {"id": "33:56/q30/p2", "position": "Ibn Masʿud adds 'as God blessed him' before the greeting.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi says it makes imitation clearer."}, {"id": "33:56/q30/p3", "position": "ʿAʾisha's codex reportedly adds 'and those who pray in the first rows.'", "reasons": "Hamida reports this before ʿUthman's codices; al-Alusi gives no grading there and denies loss of mass-transmitted Quranic text, explaining omission reports otherwise."}, {"id": "33:56/q30/p4", "position": "The common reading has the bare imperative ṣallū without fāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī prefers it as stronger because it supplies no stated cause that could invite objection."}, {"id": "33:56/q30/p5", "position": "No loss of mass-transmitted Quranic text follows from a codex-addition report.", "reasons": "Al-Murtada and al-Tabrisi argue preservation from intense memorization, ordering and tracking of differences; al-Alusi rejects attributing textual-loss doctrine to Sunnis and treats such reports as noncanonical readings, abrogated recitation or material absent at the final review."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q31", "question": "What did reports say happened when the verse came?", "turns_on": "Reports differ in occasion, speakers, ensuing verse and dating.", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q31/p1", "position": "Believers asked what honor they would receive; a verse of blessing on them followed.", "reasons": "Versions differ on whether the speaker was the Muslims, Abu Bakr or Ubayy and whether the ensuing verse was 33:43 or 9:112."}, {"id": "33:56/q31/p2", "position": "Israelites asked Moses whether God prays; the verse followed God's answer.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas versions say God told Moses that He and His angels pray for prophets and messengers."}, {"id": "33:56/q31/p3", "position": "It came in the second year after Hijra.", "reasons": "Abu Dharr al-Harawi reports this."}, {"id": "33:56/q31/p4", "position": "It came on the Night Journey.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi records and rejects this date as inconsistent with the verse's Medinan setting."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q32", "question": "How does the verse connect to its sūra and other verses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q32/p1", "position": "It follows rules against harming the Prophet and completes his honor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya says it clears suspicion about wives; Razi contrasts private household and public honor; Ibn ʿAshur sees a warning against hypocritical harm after the verse."}, {"id": "33:56/q32/p2", "position": "It parallels blessing of believers in 33:41–43 and the patient in 2:155–157.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites both; Elmalili and Kuran Yolu relate divine grace and the move from darkness to light."}]}
{"id": "33:56/q33", "question": "What ancillary material appears with these verse notes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "33:56/q33/p1", "position": "Other reports describe angels and creation honoring the Prophet.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports rocks and trees greeting him; Ibn Kathir cites angels blessing the right sides of prayer rows and an exhortation to obey the final prophet. Ibn al-Dahhan gives an unrelated account of an emphatic verbal noun."}, {"id": "33:56/q33/p2", "position": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives lexical senses of rukūʿ.", "reasons": "He cites Labid, anonymous poetry and verses for bending, abasement, prayer, bowing and prostration."}, {"id": "33:56/q33/p3", "position": "Razi discusses whether devils can enter human bodies.", "reasons": "He cites reports about bloodlike movement, objections from physical passage, harm, fire and unseen effects, then replies involving subtle bodies, divine prevention, harmless fire and choice."}, {"id": "33:56/q33/p4", "position": "Bursevi distinguishes angelic classes and human rank.", "reasons": "He describes embodied and absorbed angels, says humans unite Beauty and Majesty and reads Adam's trial as divine education."}]}

{"id": "34:24/q02", "question": "How is man yarzuqukum parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q02/p1", "position": "Man is a complete interrogative noun, nominative subject, with yarzuqukum as its predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives the case and predication."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q03", "question": "What provision comes from the heavens and earth?", "turns_on": "Whether the two realms name physical sources, God's decree and lawful acquisition, or also spiritual sustenance.", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q03/p1", "position": "Rain comes from above and vegetation, crops, fruit, or food from the earth.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Kalbi in al-Mawardi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, Bursevi, and Study Quran name rain and plants; al-Tabari adds sun, moon, stars, livelihoods, and food for humans and livestock; al-Qurtubi adds their benefits and earthly water. Islahi adds seasons to rain and growing crops as forms or means of livelihood from heaven and earth."}, {"id": "34:24/q03/p2", "position": "Heavenly provision is God's decree for His servants; earthly provision is what He permits them to take lawfully.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi offers this as an alternative to rain and vegetation."}, {"id": "34:24/q03/p3", "position": "Provision includes bodily food and inward knowledge and unveilings for spirits.", "reasons": "Bursevi says inward provision is nobler and gives enduring life, while bodily food gives passing strength; God creates and distributes both more or less widely as He wills."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q04", "question": "Why are the heavens plural here but earth singular, unlike the singular heaven in Yunus?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q04/p1", "position": "The plural points beyond the visible rain-cloud sky to higher or varied heavenly provision, while people know only one earth.", "reasons": "Al-Suhayli says they admit rain from clouds but not what lies above; al-Burhan contrasts Yunus 10:31, whose singular rests on that admission, with Saba, which supplies the answer and stresses varied provision. Al-Biqa'i says all sustenance depends on both realms and they know no other earth."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q05", "question": "What does asking who provides establish?", "turns_on": "Whether the question is read solely as proof of God's unique provision or also as a challenge about provision withheld.", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q05/p1", "position": "God alone provides, so powerless idols have no claim to worship and the sole provider deserves thanks and exclusive worship.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi cites 10:31; al-Kashshaf cites 10:31-32 and 13:16; al-Qurtubi lists rain and celestial and earthly benefits idols cannot make; Ibn Kathir links sole creation and provision to sole divinity; Ibn Ashur says divinity cannot be divided; Tabataba'i notes even idolaters recognize God alone creates provision. Al-Razi sets divine benefit here beside God's sole removal of harm in 34:22, 6:17, and 10:107; he contrasts ordinary worship for benefit with the elect's worship for God's greatness. Al-Baydawi links powerless false gods to 19:87; al-Biqa'i stresses that acknowledged provision had not produced exclusive worship. Islahi says God's command of heaven and earth demonstrates one powerful ruler; the Makkan idolaters treated their deities as intercessors rather than creators or providers."}, {"id": "34:24/q05/p2", "position": "The question also asks who could provide if God withheld His provision.", "reasons": "Study Quran cites 67:21 for this possible implication."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q06", "question": "Who supplies the answer Allah, and why is it said?", "turns_on": "Whether Allah is their actual reply, the Prophet's supplied reply to silence, or an answer demanded of them.", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q06/p1", "position": "The Prophet answers on their behalf because God is the only possible answer, though opponents may stay silent, hesitate, or refuse its implication.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says the obvious answer was first omitted and the Prophet supplies it if they profess ignorance; al-Wahidi says they can name no other provider. Al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, al-Alusi, and Tabataba'i say they inwardly assent but may not speak from stubbornness or fear of having to worship God alone. Ibn Atiyya calls them stunned; al-Razi compares acknowledgment in distress and heedlessness in ease, citing 30:33. Ibn Ashur treats Allah as their anticipated answer as at 10:31; Ibn al-Jawzi says they would give no other answer. Islahi says God supplies the answer because the addressees cannot deny it: they already acknowledge God as provider and regard their deities only as intercessors."}, {"id": "34:24/q06/p2", "position": "The Meccans themselves answer Allah, acknowledging that God provides.", "reasons": "Muqatil supplies the implied words 'we are provided' and cites 10:31. Al-Mawardi says they did not deny divine provision; al-Biqa'i and Ibn Ashur say the confession is already known."}, {"id": "34:24/q06/p3", "position": "They are ordered to answer Allah themselves so their admission becomes proof against them.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi states this as an alternative account."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q07", "question": "Why is the command qul repeated before Allah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q07/p1", "position": "The repetition heightens attention to the announced answer and the importance of proclaiming it.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says the first command already marked public proclamation as important."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q08", "question": "Where does the discourse divide after qul Allah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q08/p1", "position": "Allah closes the question and answer; an understood further 'then say' introduces the challenge over guidance.", "reasons": "Muqatil says the speech breaks there; Sahib al-Nazm in al-Wahidi makes the omitted command explicit; Ibn al-Jawzi treats Allah as the end of a sentence and the next statement as another command."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q09", "question": "Can the qaf in yarzuqukum assimilate into the kaf?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q09/p1", "position": "Yes; assimilation turns the qaf into a kaf.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas records the phonetic possibility."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q10", "question": "What is the form of inna?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q10/p1", "position": "Inna is shortened from innana by removal of one nun.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas gives this derivation."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q11", "question": "Who are we and you in the challenge?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q11/p1", "position": "We are Muhammad, his companions, or monotheists; you are the Meccan idolaters or polytheists.", "reasons": "Muqatil, al-Tha'labi, al-Mawardi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi, and al-Alusi identify these opposed camps; al-Naqqash adds that God provides for both. Al-Baydawi says the former worship the provider with intrinsic power, while the latter worship lowly inanimate things."}]}
{"id": "34:24/q12", "question": "How is iyyakum joined to inna?", "turns_on": "Whether coordination with inna's expressed subject or its syntactic position controls the scope of the guidance predicate.", "positions": [{"id": "34:24/q12/p1", "position": "Iyyakum is coordinated with the expressed subject of inna; coordination by syntactic position would use antum.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi distinguish iyyakum from 'aw antum'; al-Nahhas says the latter would restrict guidance to the first group.
